# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Although desalination is commonly believed to be too expensive for agriculture, Spain is disproving the notion
Spain has made a success of desalination, even for agricultural irrigation, despite long-standing challenges that in some cases have made it too expensive for the application. As far back as 2012, approximately 22% of desalinated water in Spain was already used for agriculture. Claudio Klynhout, of the Spanish government’s AcuaMed agency, explained:
> Here we encounter the paradox: because of the climate and the long hours of sun, there’s a great deal of tourism and very productive agriculture. And yet precisely because of the wonderful climate, there’s little water.
Spain’s long history of desalination started in the early 1960s, when many plants were built to supply drinking water, particularly in the arid Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the coast of northwestern Africa.
It soon became clear that agriculture would need desalinated water at competitive prices, and desalination plants for irrigation proliferated in the Canary Islands in the 1980s. During a water shortage in the 1990s, the desalination movement spread to the Spanish mainland with the construction of more than 200 plants.
In 2004, Spain’s AGUA (Actions for Water Management and Use) program adopted a new water policy approach more in line with the European Union’s Water Framework Directive, in which desalination is a key pillar.
Today, Spain boasts more than half of the desalination capacity of Europe. It ranks fifth worldwide with 5.7% of the world’s present desalination capacity. Today, Spain is home to 99 large capacity plants (10,000-250,000 m³/day), 450 medium capacity plants (500-10,000 m³/day), and 216 small capacity plants (100-500 m³/day). With aquifers being rapidly depleted around the world, Spain’s experience with desalination for agriculture provides a valuable model for the rest of the world.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Pros and Cons
A Spanish research team defined some of the issues and key differences between desalination for different purposes.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Desalination for Industrial Applications
Lower quality and salinity requirements for some industrial uses mean lower desalination costs in terms of personnel, chemicals, and membranes. Savings are also achieved through electrical tariffs to produce water at lower energy cost, especially for brackish water plants with large storage ponds.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Desalination for Agriculture
Agricultural desalination produces a potentially inexhaustible water supply that is not dependent on precipitation. It can increase the productivity and quality of agricultural products, consume less surface and groundwater, and allow for the recovery of salty soils.
However, there are also challenges to using desalinated water for agriculture. When it comes to treating seawater, the cost of treatment could make it unsustainable for some crops, and it can be impractical to transport the treated seawater to inland areas.
While brackish aquifers may present a new source of water for irrigation, they can become depleted just like freshwater aquifers, and brine management for such inland operations is more difficult because there is no ocean outfall.
Another challenge is that desalinated water must be ionically balanced and substances such as boron must be removed because they’re toxic to plants. Spanish researchers, however, are studying the feasibility of placing reverse osmosis systems on farms to remove boron when desalinated water from coastal plants is above crop tolerances. Researchers have found the additional cost should decrease as capacity is scaled up.

Officials on the Canary island of El Hierro hope to be a model for the future of island living, as well as an example to the rest of the world. ### Renewable energy integration for the desalination process
Increasing national targets for renewable energy use to adapt to UN Sustainable Development Goals have forced many countries to develop and implement renewable energy-powered technologies. These advances are driven by commitments made under international frameworks such as the Paris Agreement. The Middle East is distinguished by abundant solar irradiation62, making it a suitable choice for solar desalination installations. A 2016 study ranking solar desalination applicability based on water scarcity and stress, solar insolation, and saline water availability concluded that solar desalination is “highly applicable” across Middle Eastern countries63. Interestingly, almost two-thirds of the world’s deserts with maximum solar radiation are located in the Arab region64. The interest of many Middle Eastern countries in adopting renewable energy, particularly solar, to power desalination plants is therefore unsurprising, yet only six of the 17 countries currently employ or have immediate plans to integrate renewable energy with desalination, as described below.
Saudi Arabia and UAE have had photovoltaic (PV) and solar thermal systems integrated with desalination since as far back as 2008. Both countries have demonstrated their commitment to integrating renewable energy to sustainably secure water through desalination. The UAE’s ambitions in this area are evident in the commissioning of the Taweelah desalination plant, the second largest RO facility in the world with a capacity of 0.9 million m 3/day, which also integrates solar PV into its drinking water production[65](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-026-00554-x#ref-CR65 "Abu Dhabi’s Taweelah desalination plant begins operations. ### Contribution to advancing sustainable desalination
The contribution of the 17 countries to the region’s research publications in the desalination field is illustrated in Fig. 6c. The bubble size represents the contribution percentage (quantitative figures are provided in Table S4). Iran and Saudi Arabia lead in research publications, contributing around 22% each, while Yemen and Syria are at the bottom with 0.3% and 0.2%, respectively. The remaining countries fall between these extremes. These figures align with the countries’ experience in desalination, their political and economic conditions, and the growing importance of research output in academic evaluations both globally and within the region. As alluded to earlier, Saudi Arabia was among the first countries in the region to recognize the urgent need for desalination. This prompted the country to prioritize desalination research, actively directing its universities and research institutes to focus on this critical area. While Iran also hosts a significant number of desalination plants, its high volume of research publications is likely linked to the substantial increase in research output the country has experienced over the past 20 years. A report published by Stanford University revealed that Iran’s contribution to the global annual scientific output rose from 0.1% in 1997 to 2.6% in 2018 mainly driven by making academic promotion and postgraduate program completion contingent on publications[80](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-026-00554-x#ref-CR80 "Sadeh, S., Mirramezani, M., Mesgaran, M. (2019)."). Of this, about 32% was in Engineering and Environmental Sciences, fields closely related to desalination. In the cases of Yemen and Syria, several factors have impacted their desalination research output, the most significant being their heavy reliance on groundwater and surface water81,82, which has not made desalination a priority for these countries.

### Contribution to advancing sustainable desalination
The research activities related to desalination in Middle Eastern countries were supported through various funds. These funds are classified as national, regional, and international (Fig. 6d). The 12 of the 17 Middle Eastern countries—namely the six GCC nations (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman), Iran, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Turkey, and Israel were majorly supported through national funds. These funds originated through several platforms, including university research grants, laboratory/research centers, district/provincial/national departments/organizations/programs, ministries, and industries. The detailed categorical distribution of the sources is tabulated in Table S5. The regional fund in the Middle East is dominated by Saudi universities, while other regional funding bodies include the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey (TUBITAK), Qatar National Research Fund, Qatar Foundation, Middle East Desalination Research Center-Oman, Tamkeen-UAE, National Science, Technology and Innovation Plan, NSTIP- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences, and Science, Technology & Innovation Funding Authority (STDF) of Egypt. In Iraq, Cyprus, and Yemen, international funds/institutions contributed the most compared to national and regional funds. The involvement of international funds in the Middle East was counted according to two criteria: the presence of the funding body in the funding statement and the participation of at least one contributor to the research from the Middle East region. The primary international contributors were from Europe, North Asia (including China, Japan, and South Korea), and North America. The details of international funding sources that appeared in desalination-related publications are summarized in Table S6.

As shown in Fig. 7, most regional desalination innovations in the Middle East have centered around RO technology, thermal desalination using solar energy, and advancements in aiding processes (e.g., feedwater pre-treatment). This focus is logical given the transitioning of the region from thermal desalination to RO technology due to the advantageous low energy requirement of the latter compared to the former. The region’s prolonged periods of intense heat and strong sunlight each year have driven research efforts to find innovative ways to harness this energy for powering desalination facilities. According to the Global Solar Atlas, the region boasts the world’s highest potential annual photovoltaic energy output, exceeding 2800 kWh/m²[83](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-026-00554-x#ref-CR83 "Global Solar Atlas.

**Experts Urge Seawater Desalination and Investment in Water Security.**
Lebanon today faces a deepening water crisis that has been unfolding for decades, gripping the country by the throat and transforming it from the Middle East’s once-renowned “water reservoir” into a volatile epicenter of social, economic, environmental, and health crises. The nation’s so-called “white oil”, its water wealth, has become a symbol of decline and scarcity as of 2025.
The reasons are manifold, from climate change and chronic neglect to corruption, poor management, and waste. Only a small portion of Lebanon’s total water resources is usable: a mere 21%. While the renewable and potentially exploitable water resources are estimated at around 3.258 billion m³, the country’s available water today does not exceed 700 million m³ annually. Based on this trajectory, experts predict Lebanon’s water deficit could reach 1.313 billion m³ by 2030.
Lebanon’s water reality has become a blaring alarm, warning of a rapidly expanding catastrophe that demands immediate and effective solutions. While wells, mountain ponds, dams, and water trucks may offer temporary relief, specialists insist that the only real salvation lies in a comprehensive and integrated national strategy, one that addresses the root causes of the crisis and lays the groundwork for sustainable water management. Such a plan should focus on awareness, strategic planning, seawater desalination, and the implementation of progressive pricing to curb waste.
At its core, this issue is not just about water, it is about life and death for many Lebanese. It touches their health, livelihoods, and the future of their children. In this report, we delve deeper into the dimensions of the crisis, exploring its most critical components and the most effective paths toward a solution, as we document yet another growing Lebanese struggle.
**The Numbers Don’t Lie**
To grasp the full extent of the disaster, one must start with the numbers. What used to be a seasonal hardship at the end of summer has now stretched across spring and summer, forcing 80% of Lebanese citizens to buy water from trucks. Despite Lebanon’s natural richness in water resources, rainfall has dropped by 50%, and 71% of the population has faced difficulties securing their basic water needs.

Data from 2025 shows that rainfall barely reached 45 million m³, compared to an annual average of 350 million m³. Lake Qaraoun’s water levels have dropped by 65%, and the Litani River has seen a 50% decrease in flow compared to previous years. Reports indicate that around 70% of Lebanese now consume critically low amounts of water.
**Causes of the Water Crisis**
The drastic decline in water availability now threatens food security, living standards, and quality of life. Yet, this is not a recent phenomenon; its roots lie in decades of mismanagement and corruption. Alongside reduced rainfall and diminished natural reserves, a major issue is the misuse of available water resources, only 21% of the nation’s water potential is usable.
Compounding the problems are pollution of rivers, the poor maintenance of water networks, weak investment, and infrastructure leakages that waste nearly 50% of the country’s water. Add to that the drying of springs and the overuse of groundwater, which continues to deplete underground reserves.
Rapid population growth and the influx of refugees have only exacerbated the crisis, adding enormous social and economic pressures. Ultimately, poor governance and the absence of long-term planning have squandered Lebanon’s water wealth and stifled its full potential.
**The Crisis’ Fingerprints Across Lebanon**
This national water crisis carries heavy consequences across every sector: economic, environmental, health, and social.
•Economically, the crisis threatens food security, with agricultural production dropping by 30% and reliance on imported food increasing. Water-dependent industries, such as food processing and chemicals, have suffered major setbacks, and electricity generation has also been affected, all of which have deepened Lebanon’s economic woes.
•Environmentally, excessive groundwater extraction has led to the depletion and salinization of coastal aquifers. River droughts and spring reductions have damaged biodiversity and ecosystems. Without sustainable management, desertification is spreading, and green spaces are shrinking, intensifying climate change locally.
•On the health front, declining water quality, particularly from unmonitored water trucks and contaminated irrigation sources, has led to a rise in diseases such as diarrhea, food poisoning, and intestinal infections. Poor hygiene due to water shortages has also heightened risks for vulnerable groups like children and the elderly.

•Socially, water shortages have fueled local disputes, especially among farmers and residents over water distribution. The crisis has widened the social gap between those who can afford trucked water and those who cannot, triggering rural-to-urban migration and further straining urban infrastructure.
**Temporary and Fragmented Solutions**
In response, both the government and citizens have turned to stopgap measures wells, mountain ponds, trucks, and dams.
Lebanon now hosts over 40,000 wells, half of them unlicensed. While they have temporarily supplied water for irrigation and household use, they have also accelerated groundwater depletion.
Some municipalities-built mountain ponds to collect rain and snowmelt, with varying success depending on maintenance and geography.
Dams, once touted as long-term solutions, have proven problematic due to high costs, environmental risks, geological instability, and poor storage performance.
As for water trucks, they have become the main lifeline for most Lebanese, though often unregulated and unsafe, making them an emergency fix rather than a sustainable option.
**A Rescue Strategy for Sustainable Water Security**
Despite the partial success of these temporary solutions, experts stress that only a comprehensive rescue strategy can truly secure Lebanon’s water future. This national plan must unite the public and private sectors, tap into global expertise, and attract investment.
Its pillars should include:
•Modernizing and repairing water networks to curb waste and pollution.
•Investing in water infrastructure to create new water sources.
•Seawater desalination, a vital long-term solution for a coastal country like Lebanon, ideally powered by renewable energy.
•Progressive water tariffs to encourage responsible consumption.
•Public awareness campaigns highlighting water as a national and strategic resource that must be preserved.
On a structural level, experts urge investment in supply networks, dams, mountain ponds, and water treatment plants, for both seawater and wastewater and stronger quality control for all water sources. They also call for legal regulation of wells to protect groundwater reserves.
Additionally, Lebanon’s development and economic planning must integrate drought and climate change scenarios and promote the reuse of treated wastewater for agriculture and industry. Finally, administrative and legislative reforms are essential to sustain long-term sector recovery.
**A Call for Action**
This comprehensive reform package represents Lebanon’s best hope for escaping a mounting existential crisis that threatens its food, social, and environmental security. The numbers are clear and alarming, calling for swift, rational planning and sustainable management.

Every delay in implementing this rescue strategy means the continued decline of Lebanon’s “white oil.”
We have sounded the alarm, now it’s time for listening ears, strategic minds, and committed investors before thirst becomes the defining feature of Lebanon’s green landscape.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Although desalination is commonly believed to be too expensive for agriculture, Spain is disproving the notion
Spain has made a success of desalination, even for agricultural irrigation, despite long-standing challenges that in some cases have made it too expensive for the application. As far back as 2012, approximately 22% of desalinated water in Spain was already used for agriculture. Claudio Klynhout, of the Spanish government’s AcuaMed agency, explained:
> Here we encounter the paradox: because of the climate and the long hours of sun, there’s a great deal of tourism and very productive agriculture. And yet precisely because of the wonderful climate, there’s little water.
Spain’s long history of desalination started in the early 1960s, when many plants were built to supply drinking water, particularly in the arid Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the coast of northwestern Africa.
It soon became clear that agriculture would need desalinated water at competitive prices, and desalination plants for irrigation proliferated in the Canary Islands in the 1980s. During a water shortage in the 1990s, the desalination movement spread to the Spanish mainland with the construction of more than 200 plants.
In 2004, Spain’s AGUA (Actions for Water Management and Use) program adopted a new water policy approach more in line with the European Union’s Water Framework Directive, in which desalination is a key pillar.
Today, Spain boasts more than half of the desalination capacity of Europe. It ranks fifth worldwide with 5.7% of the world’s present desalination capacity. Today, Spain is home to 99 large capacity plants (10,000-250,000 m³/day), 450 medium capacity plants (500-10,000 m³/day), and 216 small capacity plants (100-500 m³/day). With aquifers being rapidly depleted around the world, Spain’s experience with desalination for agriculture provides a valuable model for the rest of the world.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Desalination for Agriculture
Agricultural desalination produces a potentially inexhaustible water supply that is not dependent on precipitation. It can increase the productivity and quality of agricultural products, consume less surface and groundwater, and allow for the recovery of salty soils.
However, there are also challenges to using desalinated water for agriculture. When it comes to treating seawater, the cost of treatment could make it unsustainable for some crops, and it can be impractical to transport the treated seawater to inland areas.
While brackish aquifers may present a new source of water for irrigation, they can become depleted just like freshwater aquifers, and brine management for such inland operations is more difficult because there is no ocean outfall.
Another challenge is that desalinated water must be ionically balanced and substances such as boron must be removed because they’re toxic to plants. Spanish researchers, however, are studying the feasibility of placing reverse osmosis systems on farms to remove boron when desalinated water from coastal plants is above crop tolerances. Researchers have found the additional cost should decrease as capacity is scaled up.

### Renewable energy integration for the desalination process
Increasing national targets for renewable energy use to adapt to UN Sustainable Development Goals have forced many countries to develop and implement renewable energy-powered technologies. These advances are driven by commitments made under international frameworks such as the Paris Agreement. The Middle East is distinguished by abundant solar irradiation62, making it a suitable choice for solar desalination installations. A 2016 study ranking solar desalination applicability based on water scarcity and stress, solar insolation, and saline water availability concluded that solar desalination is “highly applicable” across Middle Eastern countries63. Interestingly, almost two-thirds of the world’s deserts with maximum solar radiation are located in the Arab region64. The interest of many Middle Eastern countries in adopting renewable energy, particularly solar, to power desalination plants is therefore unsurprising, yet only six of the 17 countries currently employ or have immediate plans to integrate renewable energy with desalination, as described below.

•Socially, water shortages have fueled local disputes, especially among farmers and residents over water distribution. The crisis has widened the social gap between those who can afford trucked water and those who cannot, triggering rural-to-urban migration and further straining urban infrastructure.
**Temporary and Fragmented Solutions**
In response, both the government and citizens have turned to stopgap measures wells, mountain ponds, trucks, and dams.
Lebanon now hosts over 40,000 wells, half of them unlicensed. While they have temporarily supplied water for irrigation and household use, they have also accelerated groundwater depletion.
Some municipalities-built mountain ponds to collect rain and snowmelt, with varying success depending on maintenance and geography.
Dams, once touted as long-term solutions, have proven problematic due to high costs, environmental risks, geological instability, and poor storage performance.
As for water trucks, they have become the main lifeline for most Lebanese, though often unregulated and unsafe, making them an emergency fix rather than a sustainable option.
**A Rescue Strategy for Sustainable Water Security**
Despite the partial success of these temporary solutions, experts stress that only a comprehensive rescue strategy can truly secure Lebanon’s water future. This national plan must unite the public and private sectors, tap into global expertise, and attract investment.
Its pillars should include:
•Modernizing and repairing water networks to curb waste and pollution.
•Investing in water infrastructure to create new water sources.
•Seawater desalination, a vital long-term solution for a coastal country like Lebanon, ideally powered by renewable energy.
•Progressive water tariffs to encourage responsible consumption.
•Public awareness campaigns highlighting water as a national and strategic resource that must be preserved.
On a structural level, experts urge investment in supply networks, dams, mountain ponds, and water treatment plants, for both seawater and wastewater and stronger quality control for all water sources. They also call for legal regulation of wells to protect groundwater reserves.
Additionally, Lebanon’s development and economic planning must integrate drought and climate change scenarios and promote the reuse of treated wastewater for agriculture and industry. Finally, administrative and legislative reforms are essential to sustain long-term sector recovery.
**A Call for Action**
This comprehensive reform package represents Lebanon’s best hope for escaping a mounting existential crisis that threatens its food, social, and environmental security. The numbers are clear and alarming, calling for swift, rational planning and sustainable management.

### Although desalination is commonly believed to be too expensive for agriculture, Spain is disproving the notion
Spain has made a success of desalination, even for agricultural irrigation, despite long-standing challenges that in some cases have made it too expensive for the application. As far back as 2012, approximately 22% of desalinated water in Spain was already used for agriculture. Claudio Klynhout, of the Spanish government’s AcuaMed agency, explained:
> Here we encounter the paradox: because of the climate and the long hours of sun, there’s a great deal of tourism and very productive agriculture. And yet precisely because of the wonderful climate, there’s little water.
Spain’s long history of desalination started in the early 1960s, when many plants were built to supply drinking water, particularly in the arid Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the coast of northwestern Africa.
It soon became clear that agriculture would need desalinated water at competitive prices, and desalination plants for irrigation proliferated in the Canary Islands in the 1980s. During a water shortage in the 1990s, the desalination movement spread to the Spanish mainland with the construction of more than 200 plants.
In 2004, Spain’s AGUA (Actions for Water Management and Use) program adopted a new water policy approach more in line with the European Union’s Water Framework Directive, in which desalination is a key pillar.
Today, Spain boasts more than half of the desalination capacity of Europe. It ranks fifth worldwide with 5.7% of the world’s present desalination capacity. Today, Spain is home to 99 large capacity plants (10,000-250,000 m³/day), 450 medium capacity plants (500-10,000 m³/day), and 216 small capacity plants (100-500 m³/day). With aquifers being rapidly depleted around the world, Spain’s experience with desalination for agriculture provides a valuable model for the rest of the world.

### Desalination for Industrial Applications
Lower quality and salinity requirements for some industrial uses mean lower desalination costs in terms of personnel, chemicals, and membranes. Savings are also achieved through electrical tariffs to produce water at lower energy cost, especially for brackish water plants with large storage ponds.

# Desalination and Agriculture: Lessons From Spain
### Desalination for Agriculture
Agricultural desalination produces a potentially inexhaustible water supply that is not dependent on precipitation. It can increase the productivity and quality of agricultural products, consume less surface and groundwater, and allow for the recovery of salty soils.
However, there are also challenges to using desalinated water for agriculture. When it comes to treating seawater, the cost of treatment could make it unsustainable for some crops, and it can be impractical to transport the treated seawater to inland areas.
While brackish aquifers may present a new source of water for irrigation, they can become depleted just like freshwater aquifers, and brine management for such inland operations is more difficult because there is no ocean outfall.
Another challenge is that desalinated water must be ionically balanced and substances such as boron must be removed because they’re toxic to plants. Spanish researchers, however, are studying the feasibility of placing reverse osmosis systems on farms to remove boron when desalinated water from coastal plants is above crop tolerances. Researchers have found the additional cost should decrease as capacity is scaled up.

Lebanon today faces a deepening water crisis that has been unfolding for decades, gripping the country by the throat and transforming it from the Middle East’s once-renowned “water reservoir” into a volatile epicenter of social, economic, environmental, and health crises. The nation’s so-called “white oil”, its water wealth, has become a symbol of decline and scarcity as of 2025.
The reasons are manifold, from climate change and chronic neglect to corruption, poor management, and waste. Only a small portion of Lebanon’s total water resources is usable: a mere 21%. While the renewable and potentially exploitable water resources are estimated at around 3.258 billion m³, the country’s available water today does not exceed 700 million m³ annually. Based on this trajectory, experts predict Lebanon’s water deficit could reach 1.313 billion m³ by 2030.
Lebanon’s water reality has become a blaring alarm, warning of a rapidly expanding catastrophe that demands immediate and effective solutions. While wells, mountain ponds, dams, and water trucks may offer temporary relief, specialists insist that the only real salvation lies in a comprehensive and integrated national strategy, one that addresses the root causes of the crisis and lays the groundwork for sustainable water management. Such a plan should focus on awareness, strategic planning, seawater desalination, and the implementation of progressive pricing to curb waste.
At its core, this issue is not just about water, it is about life and death for many Lebanese. It touches their health, livelihoods, and the future of their children. In this report, we delve deeper into the dimensions of the crisis, exploring its most critical components and the most effective paths toward a solution, as we document yet another growing Lebanese struggle.
